questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: The Cause And The Context Are The Same Object
questions.learningObjective: read the cause and the context of a re-raised error

options.text: The two lines read TypeError outer failed then ValueError inner failed, and the three checks after them are True, True and True, because raising inside a handler sets the cause and the context to the same caught object and switches suppression on

The two lines read TypeError outer failed then ValueError inner failed, and the three checks after them are False, True and True, because naming a cause leaves the context unset while the raised object keeps its own traceback
options.misconception: believes naming a cause leaves the context unset

options.text: The two lines read TypeError outer failed then NoneType None, and the three checks after them are False, False and False, because the from clause discards the caught object entirely and leaves no traceback to inspect
options.misconception: believes the from clause discards the caught object

options.text: The two lines read TypeError outer failed then ValueError inner failed, and the three checks after them are True, True and False, because the cause is recorded but the caught object has no traceback until the replacement has been printed
options.misconception: believes the caught object has no traceback of its own

questions.explanation: A raise that happens while another exception is being handled picks that exception up as its context automatically, and naming it after the word from sets the same object as the cause on top of that. So the cause and the context end up pointing at one and the same caught object, which is why the identity check is True, and the traceback that hangs off the cause is the one built when the value error was first raised. Dropping the from clause leaves the context in place but the cause empty, and writing from None leaves the context in place and the cause empty while additionally asking the printer not to show the context, which is the difference between the two false readings above.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two recorded links are the same object, and which of them the from clause fills in.

options.text: Both lists read [25.0, 'skip', 20.0, 'skip'], the comparison is True and the length is 4, because a handler around a division always leaves the result in floating point form
options.misconception: believes a caught arithmetic fault forces floating point results

options.text: Both lists read [25, 'skip', 20, 'skip'], the comparison is True and the length is 4, because the two divisions that would divide by zero are replaced by a marker and nothing else changes

The first list reads [25, 'skip', 20, 'skip', 'skip'] and the second reads [25, 'skip', 20, 'skip'], the comparison is True and the length is 4, because the walk stops recording one step earlier than the hand-written loop does
options.misconception: believes the helper and the loop see different inputs

options.text: The first list reads [25, 20] while the second reads [25, 'skip', 20, 'skip'], the comparison is False and the length is 4, because an empty handler body drops the failing item instead of standing a marker in for it
options.misconception: believes an empty handler body drops the failing item

questions.explanation: Two of the four divisors are zero, and each of those two steps is the only thing the handler has to account for. The handler appends a marker rather than a number, so the recorded list has one slot per input and the two successful divisions keep their integer quotients of 25 and 20. An empty handler body would leave the list with two entries instead of four, which is what the last option describes, and using true division would leave the two successes as 25.0 and 20.0 with the markers still in place.
questions.hint: Count how many entries the recorded list has, and ask whether a caught fault changes the kind of number a later success produces.

questions.topic: An Unnamed Cause Becomes The Context
questions.learningObjective: tell apart the implicit context chain from an explicitly named cause

options.text: The lines read LookupError outer, RuntimeError inner, None, True and True, because raising inside a handler always hides the exception that was being handled, whether or not a cause is named
options.misconception: believes raising inside a handler always hides the handled exception

options.text: The lines read LookupError outer, RuntimeError inner, inner, True and True, because the caught runtime error becomes the cause by itself as soon as it is caught rather than when it is named
options.misconception: believes catching an error is the same as naming it as the cause

options.text: The lines read LookupError outer, RuntimeError inner, None, False and True, because the context is filled in from the handler that is running while the cause is only written when one is named after the word from
The lines read LookupError outer, RuntimeError inner, None, False and False, because the current handler information still names the exception that was running when the handler was entered
options.misconception: believes the current handler information keeps naming the earlier exception

questions.explanation: A raise performed while a handler is running always records the exception being handled as its context; nothing has to be written for that to happen. The cause slot is different: it is only filled when the raise names an exception after the word from, so here it is empty and the printed value is None while the context still holds the runtime error. The last line checks the current handler information, which names the lookup error being handled at that moment rather than the runtime error that was handled a moment earlier and has already been left behind.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two recorded links is filled in automatically and which one needs the from clause.

questions.learningObjective: see how a note list is built on an exception object

options.misconception: believes a bare raise after add_note abandons the error

options.text: The lines read 6, negative input, two note lines, False, ['now it exists', 'again'] and bare, because a second call to add_note on the same object replaces the note that was there before

The list is built up one entry at a time and a fresh exception has no such attribute at all, which is why the check on the plain error is False until a note is added and true afterwards. Printing the object shows only its message, so the notes are invisible in the last line even though the list beside it has one entry, and a second call adds a second entry rather than replacing the first.

questions.topic: One Star Handler Per Type Over A Nested Group
questions.learningObjective: follow how a star handler takes its share out of a group and leaves the rest

options.text: The six handler lines read keys 1, values 1, keys 1, values 1, values 1 and types 1, then BaseExceptionGroup and True, because each star handler removes the members that match it and leaves the rest for the handlers below, including members of a nested group

The six handler lines read keys 1, keys 1, keys 2, keys 1 and types 1, then BaseExceptionGroup and True, because a single star handler naming a tuple of types collects both of them at once and does not hand the second one to the next handler
options.misconception: believes one star handler naming two types takes both and stops there

options.text: The six handler lines read keys 1, values 1, keys 1, values 1, values 1 and types 1, then Exception and True, because the class a group of ordinary errors is built on is the ordinary error class itself
options.misconception: believes ExceptionGroup is built directly on Exception

options.text: The six handler lines show the group text instead of the member count on the first, third and fourth lines, then BaseExceptionGroup and True, because a star handler binds the single matching error rather than a group built from the matches
options.misconception: believes a star handler binds the single matching error

questions.explanation: A star handler never takes the whole group. It looks through it, including through any group nested inside it, takes the members that match the type it names, and hands what it took to the body; everything it did not take stays behind for the handlers below. That is why the third call fires two handlers in turn, once for the key error out of the nested group and once for the value error, and why the fourth call fires the value handler and then the type handler. The class printed at the end is the direct base of the group class, which is the wider base exception group rather than the ordinary error class, and that wider class is itself an ordinary error class.
questions.hint: Ask whether a star handler empties the group or only takes the members that match it.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Splitting A Group And Deriving A New One
questions.learningObjective: use split and derive on a group and read what each returns
questions.stem:
Three failures are packed into a group, the group is divided by one of the two types present, and a one-member group is then built from the result and compared with the original. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

def collect(failures):
    return ExceptionGroup("batch failed", failures)


eg = collect([ValueError("a"), TypeError("b"), ValueError("c")])
print(eg)
print(len(eg.exceptions))
print([type(e).__name__ for e in eg.exceptions])
matched, rest = eg.split(ValueError)
print(len(matched.exceptions), rest is None)
print([type(e).__name__ for e in matched.exceptions])
print(matched.message)
new = eg.derive([KeyError("x")])
print(type(new).__name__, len(new.exceptions), new.message)
print(type(new.exceptions[0]).__name__)
print(new.exceptions[0] is not eg.exceptions[0])

options.text: The lines read batch failed with 3 sub-exceptions, 3, the three type names, 3 and True, all three type names, batch failed, ExceptionGroup 1 batch failed, KeyError and True, because naming a tuple of types in the split takes every member and leaves nothing behind
options.misconception: believes naming a tuple of types in split takes every member

options.text: The lines read batch failed with 3 sub-exceptions, 3, the three type names, 2 and False, two value-error names, batch failed, ExceptionGroup 1 batch failed, KeyError and True, because splitting hands back the matches and a None for the empty remainder while deriving builds a fresh group that keeps the message

The lines read batch failed with 3 sub-exceptions, 3, the three type names, 2 and False, two value-error names, batch failed, ExceptionGroup 3 batch failed, ValueError and False, because deriving a group adds the new members to the ones the group already holds and reuses the original objects
options.misconception: believes derive adds to the group and reuses its members

options.text: The lines begin batch failed: a, b, c with 3 sub-exceptions and the derived line reads ExceptionGroup 1 batch failed: a, b, c, because the message of a group is expected to list the members it carries rather than describe the failure
options.misconception: believes the group message should list its members

questions.explanation: Splitting is a division, not a filter: it returns a group holding the matching members and, for the other side, a group if anything is left over or None if the remainder is empty. Here two of the three members match and the single type error is the whole of the remainder, so the printed pair reports two and False rather than two and a count. Deriving is the opposite operation: it builds a brand new group from the members it is given, carrying the message across but sharing no member objects with the original, which is why the last check is True.
questions.hint: Ask what splitting returns for a remainder that is empty, and whether deriving reuses the original members.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A Group Refuses To Carry A Keyboard Interrupt
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the type error raised when a narrow group is given a base-level error
questions.stem:
A group is built from one ordinary error and one interruption and then run, with the failure text and the frame that produced it both reported. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What actually happens?

import runpy
import traceback

with open("demo.py", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write("raise ExceptionGroup('mixed', [ValueError('v'), KeyboardInterrupt()])\n")

try:
    runpy.run_path("demo.py", run_name="demo")
except TypeError as exc:
    print(traceback.format_exception_only(type(exc), exc)[0].rstrip())
    frames = [fr for fr in traceback.extract_tb(exc.__traceback__) if fr.filename == "demo.py"]
    print(len(frames))
    print(frames[0].line)

options.text: The program prints TypeError: BaseExceptionGroup.__new__() argument 1 must be str, not list on the first line, then 1, then the raising line, because the two constructor arguments of a group can be supplied in either order
options.misconception: believes the group constructor takes its arguments in either order

options.text: The program prints caught ExceptionGroup 1 and then interrupt BaseExceptionGroup 1, because naming the wider group class lets the interruption sit inside it and be handed to its own star handler
options.misconception: believes the narrow group class accepts a base-level error

options.text: The program prints TypeError: Cannot nest BaseExceptions in an ExceptionGroup on the first line, then 1, then the raising line from the generated file, because the narrow group class refuses any member that is not an ordinary error and the check happens while the group is being constructed
The program prints caught ExceptionGroup 1 and then rest BaseExceptionGroup 1, because naming the wider group class makes the second star handler produce the same class as the first
options.misconception: believes a broad second star handler yields the same class as the first

questions.explanation: The narrow group class exists precisely so that a handler catching it can be sure everything inside is an ordinary error, so it refuses at construction time to hold an error that sits above that line, such as an interruption or a system exit. The refusal happens while the group object is being made, which is why the failure appears before any handler gets a chance to look at it, and why the frame reported is the one that raised rather than a handler frame. Widening the group class is the fix, and with both handlers present the value error arrives in a group of ordinary errors while the interruption arrives in a group of the wider kind.
questions.hint: Ask whether the refusal is raised while the group is being built or while a handler is running.

questions.topic: Subgroup Narrows Without Changing The Original
questions.learningObjective: read what a subgroup returns and check the original is untouched

options.text: The lines read 3, all failures with 3 sub-exceptions, ExceptionGroup 3 and all three messages twice, because a subgroup accepts a tuple of types and therefore keeps every member that was collected
options.misconception: believes a subgroup given a tuple keeps every member

options.text: The lines read 3, all failures with 2 sub-exceptions, ExceptionGroup 2 and the two value messages twice, because the only way to hold a subset of one type is to drop the rest when the group is built
options.misconception: believes filtering by type has to happen at construction

options.text: The lines read 3, all failures with 3 sub-exceptions, ExceptionGroup 1 and one value message, followed by all three messages, because a subgroup is the same as deriving a new group from a replacement list
options.misconception: believes a subgroup is the same as deriving a new list

options.text: The lines read 3, all failures with 3 sub-exceptions, ExceptionGroup 2, the two value messages and all three messages, because a subgroup builds a new group from the matching members and leaves the original group holding all three

questions.explanation: A subgroup is a read of the existing group, not an edit of it: it walks the members, keeps the ones matching the type given, and wraps those in a fresh group, leaving the original untouched. That is why the last line still shows all three messages even though the subgroup line above it shows only the two value errors, and why the member counts add up to three on both sides. Deriving is the operation that builds a group from a list you supply, so calling it here would report one member and a made-up message rather than the two that match.
questions.hint: Ask whether taking a subset changes the group it was taken from.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Reading Frames Back Out Of A Traceback
questions.learningObjective: read the filename, line number, function name and source line of a frame
questions.stem:
A small file is written to disk and run, a division by zero is caught around that run, and the frames that belong to the generated file are listed with their source lines. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import runpy
import traceback

with open("demo.py", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write("def f(a,\n      b):\n    return 1 / b\n\n\nf(1,\n   0)\n")

try:
    runpy.run_path("demo.py", run_name="demo")
except ZeroDivisionError as exc:
    print(traceback.format_exception_only(type(exc), exc)[0].rstrip())
    frames = [fr for fr in traceback.extract_tb(exc.__traceback__) if fr.filename == "demo.py"]
    for fr in frames:
        print(fr.filename, fr.lineno, fr.name, repr(fr.line))
    print(len(frames))
    print(frames[0].end_lineno - frames[0].lineno)

options.text: The lines read the division message, then demo.py 6 <module> with the text f(1,, then demo.py 3 f with the text return 1 / b, then 2 and then 1, because the call spans two source lines while the line that failed is a single line

The lines read the division message, then demo.py 6 <module> with the text f(1,, then demo.py 3 f with the text return 1 / b, then 1 and then 1, because only the frame that raised is reported for a division by zero
options.misconception: believes only the raising frame is reported

options.text: The lines read the division message, then demo.py 6 <module> and demo.py 3 f with no source text, then 2 and then 1, because a frame record carries the file and the line number but never the source text
options.misconception: believes a frame record carries no source text

options.text: The lines read the division message, then demo.py 6 <module> with the text f(1,, then demo.py 3 f with the text return 1 / b, then 2 and then 0, because the frame that spans several lines is the one that raised rather than the one that called
options.misconception: believes the last frame is the wide one

questions.explanation: There are two frames in the generated file, the module frame holding the call and the frame of the function that did the division, and each record carries the file, the line the statement starts on, the function name and the source text of that line. The call is written across two lines, so that frame starts on line 6 and ends on line 7, a span of one, while the division is on a single line of the function, whose start and end coincide and whose span is zero. The width of a frame is a property of the statement that frame was executing, not of the depth of the call.
questions.hint: Ask which frame is executing a statement that was written across more than one line.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Printing An Exception Into A Buffer
questions.learningObjective: read the shape of the text that the traceback printer produces
questions.stem:
A generated file raises a missing key, the printer is handed that error and its traceback and told to write into a buffer, and the buffer is then measured from several angles. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import io
import runpy
import traceback

with open("demo.py", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    fh.write("def f():\n    return {}['k']\n\n\nf()\n")

try:
    runpy.run_path("demo.py", run_name="demo")
except KeyError as exc:
    buf = io.StringIO()
    traceback.print_exception(type(exc), exc, exc.__traceback__, file=buf)
    text = buf.getvalue()
    print(text.count("KeyError"))
    print(text.splitlines()[0])
    print(text.splitlines()[-1])
    print("demo.py" in text)
    print("  return {}['k']" in text)
    print(len(text.splitlines()))

options.text: The lines read 1, KeyError: 'k', KeyError: 'k', False, False and 1, because the printer falls back to the error alone when it is not given a traceback object
options.misconception: believes the printer needs an explicit traceback object

options.text: The lines read 1, Traceback (most recent call last):, KeyError: 'k', True, True and 14, because the printed text is a header, a frame block, a source line and the error line, and it names both the file and the source
The lines read 1, Traceback (most recent call last):, KeyError: 'k', True, True and 12, because two of the lines in the printed text are frame separators that do not count as lines of output
options.misconception: believes two frame lines do not count as output lines

options.text: The lines read 1, Traceback (most recent call last):, the carets under the failing expression, True, True and 14, because the error line comes before the carets that mark the exact sub-expression that failed
options.misconception: believes the error line comes before the carets

questions.explanation: The printed form of a caught error is a block of text: a header line, one entry per frame with the file, the line number and the source line, and then the error type and message on the final line. In this case the message repeats the word that names the type, so the search for that word finds it once in the source and once on the final line only if the two spellings differ, and the search here reports a single hit because the printed source does not contain it. The file name and the exact source line both appear, which is what makes the text useful for locating the fault, and the number of lines follows from the single frame this file has.
questions.hint: Count the lines by their role: one header, one frame entry, one source line, one final error line.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: An Exit Stack Unwinds In Reverse
questions.learningObjective: order nested managers and stack callbacks as a block is left
questions.stem:
Two nested managers are opened around a piece of work, and then a stack registers one callback, two managers and a second callback around another piece of work. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import contextlib


class Recorder:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.events = []

    @contextlib.contextmanager
    def step(self, label):
        self.events.append("start:" + label)
        try:
            yield self
        finally:
            self.events.append("end:" + label)


def body(r):
    with r.step("outer"):
        with r.step("inner"):
            r.events.append("work")


r = Recorder("r")
body(r)
print(r.events)
print(len(r.events))

r2 = Recorder("r2")
with contextlib.ExitStack() as stack:
    stack.callback(r2.events.append, "first callback")
    for label in ("a", "b"):
        stack.enter_context(r2.step(label))
    stack.callback(r2.events.append, "last callback")
    r2.events.append("bulk")
print(r2.events)

options.text: The first two lines are the same and the third line places the last callback just after the two starts, because appending to the event list at that point is the same as registering it to run when the stack is released
options.misconception: believes appending to a list is the same as registering a callback

options.text: The first two lines read the nested start, work and end marks in start, work, end, end order with a count of 5, and the third line ends with the first callback, because everything registered on a stack is released in the reverse of the order it was registered
The first two lines are the same and the third line begins with the start marks in the order b then a, because managers entered in a loop unwind in the same order they were entered
options.misconception: believes stack cleanup follows entry order

options.text: The first line ends with two start marks and the third line ends with two more start marks, because the cleanup part of a manager runs the same body as the entry part
options.misconception: believes the cleanup part repeats the entry body

questions.explanation: Managers nest the way blocks do: the inner one is released before the outer one, so the end marks appear in the reverse of the start marks. A stack keeps that same discipline for everything registered on it, so the callback registered first is the last one to run and the callback registered last is the first to run after the managers are released, with the manager end marks in between in reverse entry order. A plain append to the event list is a statement that runs at that moment rather than a registration, so it appears early in the list instead of at the end.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two orders a stack uses, and whether an append is a registration.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Redirecting Output And Suppressing A Failure
questions.learningObjective: see what a redirect captures and what a suppressor lets through
questions.stem:
Two prints are sent into a buffer that replaces the ordinary output stream, one print to the error stream goes into a second buffer, and a missing key is looked up inside a block that is meant to absorb that one failure. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import contextlib
import io
import sys

buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
    print("captured")
    print("also captured")
print("outside")
print(repr(buf.getvalue()))

err = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stderr(err):
    print("oops", file=sys.stderr)
print(repr(err.getvalue()))

with contextlib.suppress(KeyError, IndexError):
    {}["missing"]
print("still here")

options.text: The lines read outside, the captured text with one line, the error text with one line, and still here, because a redirect replaces the stream rather than adding to it, so only the first print is kept
options.misconception: believes a redirect keeps only the first print

options.text: The four lines read the captured text with three lines, the error text with one line, and still here, because the block ends at the last line inside it rather than at the line that is indented less
options.misconception: believes the block ends at the last indented line

options.text: The lines read outside, the captured text with two lines, the error text with one line, and still here, because the redirect is undone when the block ends and the suppressor swallows the failure without ending the block
The lines read outside, the captured text with two lines, then the captured text again, and still here, because both streams are restored from the same buffer once the first block has ended
options.misconception: believes both streams restore from the same buffer

questions.explanation: A redirect swaps the stream object for the duration of the block and puts the original one back when the block is left, so the print after the block goes to the real output and the buffer holds exactly the two lines written inside. The same is true of the error stream, which is why the second buffer holds only the line that was sent to it. A suppressor is different: it catches the named errors and lets the block carry on to its end, so the statement after the failing lookup still runs and the failure leaves no mark other than its absence.
questions.hint: Ask when the original stream comes back, and whether a suppressed error stops the rest of the block.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Recording Warnings And Pointing At The Caller
questions.learningObjective: record warnings in a list and read the category, message and reported line
questions.stem:
A helper reports that it is deprecated and returns a doubled value, and its two calls are made inside a block that records every warning rather than printing it. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import warnings


def old_api(n):
    warnings.warn("old_api is deprecated", DeprecationWarning, stacklevel=2)
    return n * 2


with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    print(old_api(3))
    print(old_api(4))
    print(len(caught))
    print(caught[0].category.__name__)
    print(str(caught[0].message))
    print(caught[0].filename.endswith("prog.py"))
    print(caught[0].lineno)

options.text: The lines read 6, 8, 2, DeprecationWarning, old_api is deprecated, True and 5, because a stack level of two still points the record at the line inside the helper that reported the warning
options.misconception: believes the stack level has no effect on the reported line

options.text: The lines read 6, 8, 4, DeprecationWarning, old_api is deprecated, True and 11, because the recorded list holds one entry per call to the helper rather than one entry per warning
options.misconception: believes the list holds one entry per call

options.text: The lines read 6, 8, 2, UserWarning, old_api is deprecated, True and 11, because a message that does not name a category is filed under the general user warning
options.misconception: believes the message overrides the named category

options.text: The lines read 6, 8, 2, DeprecationWarning, old_api is deprecated, True and 11, because a stack level of two points the record at the line that called the helper rather than the line that reported it

questions.explanation: A report is a message plus a category plus a place, and the place is chosen by counting frames outward from the statement that reported it. A stack level of one is the reporting line inside the helper and a stack level of two is the line that called it, which here is the first of the two print statements. The two calls each produce one record, so the list has two entries, and the first of those records the category that was named rather than the general one used when no category is given.
questions.hint: Ask how many frames the stack level of two skips, and what category the record carries.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Turning A Warning Into A Failure
questions.learningObjective: compare the error, ignore and default warning filters by running them
questions.stem:
One helper reports a warning, and the same helper is then called under three different filters in three separate recording blocks. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import warnings


def check():
    warnings.warn("value is nearly gone", RuntimeWarning)
    return 1


with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("error")
    try:
        check()
    except RuntimeWarning as exc:
        print("raised", type(exc).__name__, exc)
    print(len(caught))

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    check()
    print("ignored", len(caught))

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("default")
    check()
    check()
    print("default once", len(caught))

options.text: The lines read raised RuntimeWarning value is nearly gone, 0, ignored 0 and default once 1, because the error filter turns the warning into a real failure that is caught rather than recorded, and the default filter reports a given warning from a given line only once
The lines read 0, ignored 0 and default once 1, because a warning raised under the error filter is recorded like any other warning and nothing is raised
options.misconception: believes the error filter records the warning instead of raising it

options.text: The lines read raised RuntimeWarning value is nearly gone, 0, ignored 0 and default once 2, because the default filter reports a repeated warning on every call rather than only the first
options.misconception: believes the default filter reports every repetition

options.text: The lines read raised RuntimeWarning value is nearly gone, 0, ignored 0 and default once 1, because the error filter still leaves one record behind even when the warning is turned into a failure
options.misconception: believes the error filter leaves a record behind

questions.explanation: The error filter changes what a warning is: instead of being filed and ignored it is raised as the warning class itself, so the surrounding block catches it as an ordinary error and the recording list stays empty. The ignore filter does the opposite and files nothing, so that block reports a count of zero without any failure reaching the caller. The default filter sits between them: it files the first report from a given line and then stays quiet for the same report from the same line, which is why two calls from one line produce a single record.
questions.hint: Ask what the error filter does to the object the warning call would have returned.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: The Default Filter And Its Per Line Memory
questions.learningObjective: read the default filter entry and the repetition rule it applies
questions.stem:
A helper that reports a message is called three times under a filter that files everything, and the two members of the first filter entry are printed before any of that. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import warnings


def emit(text):
    warnings.warn(text)


print(warnings.filters[0][0])
print(warnings.filters[0][2].__name__)

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    emit("repeated")
    emit("repeated")
    emit("other")
    print(len(caught))
    print([w.message.args[0] for w in caught])
    print(caught[0].lineno)
    print(caught[0].filename.endswith("prog.py"))

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("default")
    emit("repeated")
    emit("repeated")
    print("default", len(caught))

options.text: The lines read default, DeprecationWarning, 2, two messages, 5, True and default 1, because reporting the same message twice from one line is treated as a single report
options.misconception: believes identical messages collapse under the always filter

options.text: The lines read default, DeprecationWarning, 3, the three messages, 5, True and default 1, because the first filter entry handles the deprecation category with the default action, and the default action files only the first report from a given line
The lines read default, DeprecationWarning, 3, three category names, 5, True and default 1, because each record holds the category rather than the message that was reported
options.misconception: believes a record holds the category rather than the message

options.text: The lines read default, DeprecationWarning, 3, the three messages, 5, True and default 2, because the recording block starts from the default filter rather than from a filter of its own
options.misconception: believes the recording block inherits the default filter

questions.explanation: A filter entry is a list whose first member is the action and whose third member is the category it covers, and the entry that ships first covers the deprecation category with the default action. Under a filter that files everything, each of the three calls produces its own record, so the two identical messages both appear in the message list. Under the default action the same message from the same line is filed only the first time, so the second block, which calls twice from one line, reports a single record. The reported line is the line inside the helper, since no stack level was given, and it is line five of the file.
questions.hint: Ask what the second member of a recorded warning is, and what the default action does on a repeat from one line.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A Custom Error Carries Its Own Fields
questions.learningObjective: read the message, the stored fields and the cause of a custom error

options.text: The lines read ok, stage load failed, load, KeyError with the quoted message, the single-element tuple and False, because the cause slot is only filled when the error is re-raised rather than when a new one is raised from it
options.misconception: believes the cause slot stays empty for a new error raised from another

options.text: The lines read ok, stage load failed, load, KeyError with the unquoted message, the single-element tuple and True, because a stored cause prints as its message rather than as the way the interpreter shows it
options.misconception: believes a stored cause prints as its message

options.text: The lines read ok, stage load failed, load, KeyError with the quoted message, the single-element tuple and True, because the base call fixes the message and the argument tuple, and naming the cause puts the same object in the cause slot as in the stored field

The lines read ok, stage load failed, load, KeyError with the quoted message, the single-element tuple and False, because the cause slot points at the new error rather than at the error that was being handled
options.misconception: believes the cause slot points at the new error

questions.explanation: Calling the base constructor with one message fixes both the text the error prints and the argument tuple the interpreter keeps, so the tuple has exactly one entry even though the subclass stores two extra fields of its own. The fields set on the object are ordinary attributes and have nothing to do with that tuple. Raising the new error from the caught one writes the caught object into the cause slot, and since the same object was also stored as a field, the identity check between the two is True. Printing the caught error shows the way the interpreter renders a key error, which is its type name followed by the quoted key rather than the bare key.
questions.hint: Ask what the base constructor call puts in the argument tuple, and whether the cause and the stored field are the same object.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Walking The Links Of A Traceback
questions.learningObjective: walk a traceback link by link and read the frames it visits
questions.stem:
Four functions are nested so that the innermost one raises, the whole printed form is measured, and then the traceback is walked one link at a time from the outside in. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import traceback


def inner():
    raise ValueError("deepest")


def middle():
    inner()


def outer():
    middle()


try:
    outer()
except ValueError as exc:
    text = "".join(traceback.format_exception(type(exc), exc, exc.__traceback__))
    body = [ln for ln in text.splitlines() if ln.strip().startswith("File")]
    print(len(body))
    for ln in body:
        print(ln.split(", in ")[-1])
    print(text.splitlines()[-1])
    tb = exc.__traceback__
    names = []
    while tb is not None:
        names.append(tb.tb_frame.f_code.co_name)
        tb = tb.tb_next
    print(names)
    print(tb is None)

options.text: The lines read 4, the four function names outermost first, ValueError: deepest, two names and True, because each link skips the frame between it and the next one outward
options.misconception: believes each link skips a frame

options.text: The lines read 4, the four function names outermost first, Traceback (most recent call last):, the same four names as a list and True, because the header line is the last line of the printed form rather than the first
options.misconception: believes the header comes last

options.text: The lines read 13, every line of the printed form in order ending with the error line twice, the same four names as a list and True, because every printed line belongs to the frame block and none of them is a header
options.misconception: believes every printed line is a frame line

options.text: The lines read 4, the four function names outermost first, ValueError: deepest, the same four names as a list and True, because each link points at the next frame outward from the point of failure and the walk ends when the last link is None

questions.explanation: A traceback is a linked list whose first link is the frame where the failure happened and whose last link has nothing after it, so walking it visits the innermost function first and ends at the module frame. Reading each link gives the code object of that frame, whose name is the function that was running, and the four names come out outermost first because the printed form lists them in that order even though the links run the other way. The printed form has one line per frame plus a header and a final error line, and after the walk the pointer is None, which is what the last line reports.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the links run in, and what the pointer holds once the walk is finished.
